To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) SLN biopsy is a safe, effective and accurate method of staging the axilla, with a low false‐negative rate and a low rate of axillary lymph node recurrence; 2) the use of a blue dye and/or a radiotracer improves SLN detection rates; 3) SLN detection rates are improved when the procedure is performed by experienced surgeons and when the procedure is carried out in centres performing a high number of SLN biopsies; 4)
the use of intraoperative analysis of sentinel nodes in breast cancer patients with clinically negative nodes can reduce the number of patients undergoing axillary lymph node dissection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel intraoperative imaging technique for sentinel lymph node biopsy in breast cancer patients.
the use of intraoperative assessment of sentinel nodes for breast cancer.
the development, validation and implementation of intraoperative techniques for the detection of sentinel lymph nodes and the analysis of the sentinel node for metastases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
intraoperative assessment of sentinel nodes is not yet ready for routine use in the UK, and further work is required to determine its place in breast cancer surgery.
intraoperative assessment of sentinel nodes in breast cancer is feasible, but the evidence is insufficient to make recommendations for its routine use.
intraoperative assessment of the sentinel lymph nodes during breast cancer surgery is not yet standard of care and should only be used in the context of a clinical trial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
intraoperative assessment of sentinel nodes in breast cancer is feasible and safe, but the clinical benefits remain to be proven in a randomised controlled trial.
the intraoperative assessment of sentinel nodes is safe, reliable and feasible, and should be considered for all patients with clinically node-negative breast cancer.
we have demonstrated the feasibility of using a handheld probe to identify the sentinel lymph node during breast surgery.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of a combination of the two most commonly used tracers, isosulfan blue and technetium‐99, is safe, and the use of a handheld gamma probe can improve the detection rate of sentinel lymph nodes.

the intraoperative assessment of sentinel nodes can be performed with a high degree of accuracy and that this approach can be applied to a large number of patients with breast cancer, including those with large primary tumours.
the sentinel node biopsy is an accurate method to stage the axilla in breast cancer, with a high rate of false‐negative results.
